newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish ambassadors calm over NATO, EU prospects.
newsitem.headline: Polish ambassadors calm over NATO, EU prospects.

text.p: Polish ambassadors to EU and NATO states agreed in Warsaw on Thursday that there was no serious danger to their country's progress towards entering both organisations, despite some clouds on the horizon.

Foreign minister Dariusz Rosati said prospects for NATO entry were on track even though there were some opposing voices in several of the 16 member states, all parliaments of which must ratify the Western defence pact's expansion.

"On the question of ratification difficulties, from what we have heard at our meeting...there are no reasons for special fears," Rosati told reporters after a first session with the 24 ambassadors and Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.

Rosati expressed surprise over reports that Naphtali Lavie, vice-president of the Israel-based World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO), had vowed to use all available means to block Polish, Czech and Romanian membership of NATO.
The WJRO passed a resolution to this effect in a meeting in Jerusalem on Monday.

The WJRO, linked with the U.S.-based World Jewish Congress, argues that these countries have not done enough to restore Jewish property taken over by communist authorities after the German-inflicted Holocaust during World War Two.
Poland is conscious that Jewish opinion has influence in the U.S. Senate, where a two-thirds majority will be needed to confirm enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

Rosati said Poland had tried to meet Jewish suggestions through a recent law paving the way for a return of property to Jewish communities and by a plan to improve conservation of the former Auschwitz-Birkenau death camp, where up to 1.5 million Jews were murdered by German invaders.
Rosati said the entry of Poland and other Central European countries to NATO was a chance to break a curse long weighing on Europe and he hoped all politicians understood this.

"I don't think any other matters, no matter how justified...could in any way influence the realisation of this absolutely top priority enterprise -- building a new system of security and a united Europe," he said.

Poland, which escaped Moscow's domination after the 1989 fall of communism, wants to bind itself to the West quickly and Rosati said last month's agreement between Russia and NATO had undermined key arguments of Western opponents of NATO growth.

The ambassadors were meeting to discuss crucial coming events, notably NATO's Madrid summit in July, at which a first group including at least Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are expected to be invited to start entry talks.
A European Union summit in Amsterdam this month, concluding the current Inter-governmental conference, is also likely to pave the way for talks on enlargement to start early next year.

Polish officials have said that an opinion or "avis" the EU's executive European Commission is soon to give on countries' preparations to join may contain some criticisms, but Rosati said these would apply to all candidate states.
"I don't think that the avis...will in any way threaten Poland's place in the first group of countries invited for membership negotiations," Rosati said.
